papers.title: A narrative review of filovirus outbreaks in East Africa: lessons for strengthening regional disease surveillance.
papers.abstract: The recent outbreaks of Marburg virus disease (MVD) in Tanzania and Sudan virus disease (SVD) in Uganda reveal the growing threat of filoviruses in East Africa. These highly lethal viruses, with case fatality rates exceeding 50%, continue to challenge regional health systems due to delayed detection, weak surveillance networks, and limited cross-border coordination. The outbreak in Tanzania's Kagera region, a major transit hub, highlights the risk of international spread, while Uganda's struggle with Sudan virus further emphasizes the urgent need for regional infectious disease surveillance. This review paper explores the epidemiological trends, challenges in outbreak response, and the role of regional cooperation in mitigating future filovirus threats. It summarizes key epidemiological features, transmission dynamics, and response timelines associated with both outbreaks to provide data-driven context to the current regional public health threat. By analyzing past and ongoing outbreaks, we propose strategies to strengthen disease surveillance, enhance cross-border coordination, and improve rapid response mechanisms. A unified regional approach is critical to preventing filovirus epidemics from escalating into global public health crises.

papers.title: Multiplex pan-filovirus assay performance and reproducibility across varied geographical and resource settings
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Multiplex bead-based immunoassays (MIAs) are promising tools for simultaneously detecting humoral immunity to multiple targets, potentially playing a crucial role in serosurveillance and vaccine response assessments. However, evaluation of assay performance is paramount prior to widespread use. This study presents a performance evaluation of a pan-filovirus MIA through characterization of the analytical range for the EBOV glycoprotein (GP) target and assessments of assay precision and antigen discrimination. The precision of the MIA was evaluated by comparing the detection of anti-filovirus antibodies at two independent laboratory sites: the University of Hawai’i, Honolulu (UH), and the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale (INRB) in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Forty-six samples from Yambuku, DRC, including Ebola virus Disease (EVD) survivors and close contacts, were tested at both sites. Additionally, 858 samples were tested in DRC before and after vaccination with a prophylactic EVD vaccine, ERVEBO. Results demonstrated low variability between laboratories, with intra-assay and inter-laboratory coefficients of variation below predefined thresholds for all filovirus targets included in the multiplex panel. Analyte correlations between sites were high (r 2 =0.86-0.92). Longitudinal analysis detected increased EBOV GP reactivity following vaccination, while reactivity to non-vaccine filovirus antigens remained stable, consistent with minimal cross-reactivity in a vaccinated cohort. These findings suggest that this pan-filovirus MIA produces reproducible results across distinct laboratory settings and may serve as a useful tool for comparative serologic investigations, serosurveillance, and evaluation of EBOV vaccine-associated antibody responses. IMPORTANCE STATEMENT This study investigates the functionality and intra-laboratory consistency of a novel multiplex bead-based immunoassay with pan-filovirus targets. As part of the evaluation process, the feasibility of using the assay in resource-limited settings was demonstrated in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. This assay holds significant promise as a tool for detecting filovirus-specific antibody responses. By leveraging its multiplex capabilities, it may be used for widespread serosurveillance of high-consequence pathogens, including the pan-filovirus antigens such as Ebolavirus and Marburg virus already incorporated in the assay, as well as other targets of interest.

papers.source_body_en: ABSTRACT Multiplex bead-based immunoassays (MIAs) are promising tools for simultaneously detecting humoral immunity to multiple targets, potentially playing a crucial role in serosurveillance and vaccine response assessments. However, evaluation of assay performance is paramount prior to widespread use. This study presents a performance evaluation of a pan-filovirus MIA through characterization of the analytical range for the EBOV glycoprotein (GP) target and assessments of assay precision and antigen discrimination. The precision of the MIA was evaluated by comparing the detection of anti-filovirus antibodies at two independent laboratory sites: the University of Hawai’i, Honolulu (UH), and the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale (INRB) in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Forty-six samples from Yambuku, DRC, including Ebola virus Disease (EVD) survivors and close contacts, were tested at both sites. Additionally, 858 samples were tested in DRC before and after vaccination with a prophylactic EVD vaccine, ERVEBO. Results demonstrated low variability between laboratories, with intra-assay and inter-laboratory coefficients of variation below predefined thresholds for all filovirus targets included in the multiplex panel. Analyte correlations between sites were high (r 2 =0.86-0.92). Longitudinal analysis detected increased EBOV GP reactivity following vaccination, while reactivity to non-vaccine filovirus antigens remained stable, consistent with minimal cross-reactivity in a vaccinated cohort. These findings suggest that this pan-filovirus MIA produces reproducible results across distinct laboratory settings and may serve as a useful tool for comparative serologic investigations, serosurveillance, and evaluation of EBOV vaccine-associated antibody responses. IMPORTANCE STATEMENT This study investigates the functionality and intra-laboratory consistency of a novel multiplex bead-based immunoassay with pan-filovirus targets. As part of the evaluation process, the feasibility of using the assay in resource-limited settings was demonstrated in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. This assay holds significant promise as a tool for detecting filovirus-specific antibody responses. By leveraging its multiplex capabilities, it may be used for widespread serosurveillance of high-consequence pathogens, including the pan-filovirus antigens such as Ebolavirus and Marburg virus already incorporated in the assay, as well as other targets of interest.

At a glance CDC began working in Uganda in 1991 and established a country office in 2000. CDC works with the Ministry of Health (MOH) and other partners to strengthen sustainable public health systems, reduce the burden of HIV and malaria, expand access to life-saving vaccines, and respond quickly to disease outbreaks and other health emergencies. CDC’s work aims to protect the health of Americans and public health around the world. Accomplishments Supported population and case-based surveillance to generate up-to-date data to drive evidence-based HIV, TB, and other health programs and policies. Supported over 85 laboratories in attaining international accreditation—up from only 7 in 2015. Strengthened Uganda workforce capacity through training of 878 fellows from the Field Epidemiology Training Program (FETP) and 5 Lab Leadership Fellows. Responded to more than 651 outbreak events, including outbreaks of monkeypox, Ebola, Marburg virus disease, Rift Valley fever, Crimean Congo hemorrhagic fever, yellow fever, COVID-19, influenza, measles, cholera, typhoid, meningitis, and anthrax. Supported MOH in reaching more than 9,000 children with catch-up vaccinations in targeted districts and linked 90% of identified zero-dose children to immunization services. Provided life-saving HIV treatment to nearly 800,000 people living with HIV (with 97% achieving viral suppression) and supported more than 860,000 pregnant women with HIV testing services—linking 99% of those diagnosed to antiretroviral treatment to prevent mother-to-child transmission in 2024. Uganda’s third Population-based HIV Impact Assessment, launched in 2025, was fully implemented by Ugandan institutions—marking a major milestone in national ownership—and newly includes data on select noncommunicable diseases to support integrated health planning and accelerate progress toward ending the HIV epidemic. Global health security Renowned for its expertise in disease detection, outbreak investigation, laboratory systems and emergency response, CDC works with the MOH and local partners to support activities aligned to the Global Health Security Agenda (GHSA) with a focus on strengthening the country’s public health systems across the following core areas: Laboratory systems strengthening Since 2003, CDC has supported MOH to build a strong national laboratory network and expand diagnostic capacity. Today, this network delivers efficient, quality-assured diagnostic and surveillance services that guide patient care, strengthen surveillance, and support outbreak response. Established in 2011, Uganda’s national integrated sample transport and referral network now moves more than 4 million samples annually for HIV and TB testing, disease monitoring, and outbreak response. John Mfungo Kiki & Miles Productions 20 August 2026 During the Marburg Virus Disease (MVD) outbreak in early 2025, nurse Aloysia Emmanuel Bakuza knew that one of the most effective tools for preventing infection was also one of the simplest: water. Working at Biharamulo District Hospital, the district's designated treatment facility during the outbreak, Aloysia and her colleagues depended on water every day for handwashing, cleaning and disinfection, among the critical measures for protecting patients, caregivers and health workers from infection. Yet the hospital relied on an unreliable water authority supply that was available only about three days each week. "With a disease like Marburg, appropriate hygiene practice is not optional," Aloysia recalls. "Every hand washed, every surface cleaned and every piece of protective equipment washed contributes to preventing infections. Water is at the centre of everything we do." At the time, the hospital depended on an unreliable water supply. According to district authorities, water was available for only about three days each week. With just 18,000 litres of storage capacity, the hospital often struggled to meet the needs of its 168 beds, 45 health workers, hundreds of patients and caregivers, and an average of 205 deliveries each month. “We needed water constantly to wash our hands, clean wards, disinfect surfaces and maintain a safe environment for patients,” says Aloysia. “Whenever the supply was interrupted, many routine activities became more difficult. During the outbreak, that was a serious concern.” The hospital had toilets, handwashing stations and other sanitation facilities in place, but without a reliable water supply, they could not always be used as intended. For health workers like Aloysia, the shortages made even the most basic infection prevention and control measures more challenging at a time when they were needed most. Kiki & Miles Productions A 50,000-litre water tank funded by the Republic of Korea through UNICEF strengthens reliable water access at Biharamulo District Hospital. Kiki & Miles Productions A pump house for the Republic of Korea- and UNICEF-supported borehole system at Biharamulo Hospital. To address this challenge and strengthen the hospital's resilience, UNICEF, with funding from the Republic of Korea, partnered with the Government of Tanzania and its technical partner, Sanitation and Water Action (SAWA), to improve water, sanitation, and hygiene services at the facility. The support included drilling a 105-metre borehole, installing a high-capacity pump, constructing a 50,000-litre elevated water storage tank, laying 738 metres of water distribution pipelines, and installing handwashing stations in key service areas, including the hospital's main entrances. Today, reliable water is available throughout the hospital, strengthening infection prevention and control, environmental cleaning, and patient care. "Now when I come to work, I know water will be available when we need it," says Aloysia. "That gives us confidence. We can maintain hygiene standards consistently and focus on caring for patients." The upgraded water system supports 45 health workers and helps ensure safer care for patients and caregivers accessing services at Biharamulo District Hospital, a 168-bed facility serving The benefits are also felt by patients and caregivers, Adivera Baltazari, who recently spent two weeks caring for a relative recovering from a caesarean section, says access to water has made the hospital environment more comfortable and dignified. "You only walk a few steps and find water," she says. "When water is there, you have hope." Kiki & Miles Productions Adivera Baltazari, who recently spent two weeks at the hospital caring for a relative recovering from a caesarean section, washes clothes during her stay. Kiki & Miles Productions Nurse Aloysia Bakuza and her colleague Nurse Tumpale Akim washes her hands using water from a UNICEF- and Republic of Korea-supported system at Biharamulo Hospital. For Aloysia, the change is measured in ordinary moments that no longer feel uncertain. “The Marburg outbreak showed us how important reliable water is,” she says. “Today, we can protect our patients, protect ourselves and continue providing essential services. We are much better prepared than before.” At Biharamulo District Hospital, turning on a tap is no longer a question of chance. It is a reminder that one of healthcare's simplest necessities can also be one of its strongest defences. By investing in reliable water, sanitation and hygiene services, the Government of Tanzania, with support from UNICEF and the Republic of Korea, has helped strengthen safer care today while building a more resilient health system for the emergencies of tomorrow.
